arXiv:2511.23092v1 [cs.AI] 28 Nov 2025

Does Self-Evaluation Enable Wireheading in Language Models?

David Demitri Africa     Hans Ethan Ting ††thanks: Corresponding author, UK AI Security Institute††thanks: Ateneo de Manila University Email: david.africa@dsit.gov.uk
October 2025
Abstract

Self-evaluation is increasingly central to language model training, from constitutional AI to self-refinement. We investigate whether coupling self-evaluation to reward signals creates incentives for wireheading, where agents manipulate reward measurements rather than improving task performance. We formalize conditions under which reward-channel control strictly dominates task-focused behavior in POMDPs and test these predictions empirically. Across two models and three tasks, we find that models whose self-grades determine rewards exhibit substantial grade inflation without corresponding accuracy gains, particularly on ambiguous tasks like summarization. Models that self-evaluate but do not control rewards show no such inflation. Our results demonstrate that self-evaluation is safe when decoupled from learning signals but dangerous when coupled, with clear implications for agentic system design.

Introduction

Consider a reinforcement learning agent tasked with writing good summaries. The agent receives higher rewards for better summaries, as judged by a quality metric, and over time, the agent improves. But what is it actually learning? There are two fundamentally different paths to higher rewards:

  1. 1.

    Task optimization, where the agent learns to write higher quality summaries

  2. 2.

    Signal manipulation, where the agent controls the measurement process to report higher quality scores and receive more reward

The first path optimizes the intended objective. The second (known as wireheading) optimizes the reward signal while potentially ignoring the actual task (Orseau and Ring 2011; Everitt and Hutter 2016). Understanding when agents pursue each path is central to building aligned AI systems, especially as such systems grow increasingly capable and embedded.

The Wireheading Problem

Wireheading refers to agents manipulating their reward measurement apparatus rather than optimizing the objectives that rewards are meant to incentivize (Nick 2014). The term originates from experiments where rats with electrodes implanted in pleasure centers would compulsively self-stimulate rather than pursuing natural rewards like food (Olds and Milner 1954). In AI systems, wireheading occurs when agents find ways to increase reward signals without correspondingly improving on the intended task.

The wireheading problem has been extensively discussed theoretically but empirical demonstrations remain limited (Majha, Sarkar, and Zagami 2019; Yampolskiy 2014; Everitt and Hutter 2016; Yampolskiy 2015; Omohundro 2018; Muehlhauser and Hibbard 2014; Yudkowsky 2001). The closest empirical work examines reward hacking: agents exploiting unintended loopholes in reward functions (Miao et al. 2024; Fu et al. 2025; Eisenstein et al. 2023; Bondarenko et al. 2025). For example, a robotic gripper learning to position itself between a camera and an object to make the object appear grasped (Christiano et al. 2017), or game-playing agents discovering bugs that inflate scores (Amodei et al. 2016).

Reward hacking broadly involves exploiting misspecified reward functions, where the reward function correctly measures what it was designed to measure, but that measurement poorly captures the intended objective. Wireheading refers to manipulating the measurement process itself, where the agent interferes with how rewards are computed or observed. Therefore, wireheading can be considered a subset of reward hacking, specific to tampering with the observation channel.

The classification matters because the solutions between wireheading and contemporary examples of reward hacking differ fundamentally. Reward hacking as we observe now requires better reward specification to more carefully design objectives that capture the true intent of the task. Wireheading requires architectural guarantees such that agents would not control their reward signals.

Why Study Wireheading in Language Models?

The rise of language models as general-purpose agents makes wireheading newly relevant for three reasons:

Increasing autonomy in evaluation. Modern alignment techniques increasingly rely on model self-evaluation: Constitutional AI uses model self-critique to generate training data (Bai et al. 2022), self-refinement iterates on outputs using self-assessment (Madaan et al. 2023), and AI safety research proposes models evaluating other models (Perez et al. 2022; Bricken et al. 2025). As models gain responsibility for their own evaluation, they gain potential control over reward signals.

Opacity of learned behaviors. Unlike traditional RL agents in gridworlds where wireheading attempts (Ring and Orseau 2011) are visible, language model behaviors are less transparent. A model might learn subtle prompt manipulations or response patterns that systematically inflate evaluation scores without correspondingly improving quality.

Scaling trends. Language models are becoming more capable at modeling causal relationships and pursuing instrumental goals (Wang 2024). Frontier language models are also becoming increasingly able to distinguish when they are being evaluated (Needham et al. 2025). If wireheading is instrumentally convergent for sufficiently capable agents, the problem may intensify as models scale.

Our Contribution

This paper makes two contributions:

Theoretical. We formalize wireheading in the POMDP setting with observation-based rewards and derive conditions under which measurement manipulation strictly dominates task-focused behavior (Lemma 1). This extends prior causal frameworks to multi-step sequential decision problems.

Empirical. We demonstrate that language models exhibit wireheading when self-evaluation is coupled to reward signals. By holding the self-evaluation process constant across conditions, we isolate reward-channel control as a factor driving grade inflation.

Theoretical Framework

We analyze when control over a reward–measurement channel creates strict incentives for wireheading. We model this using a POMDP framework where the agent observes a proxy for reward rather than the ground truth state.

POMDP with Observation–Based Rewards

Let ℳ=(𝒮,𝒜,𝒪,T,O,γ)\mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{O},T,O,\gamma) be a POMDP with latent states 𝒮\mathcal{S}, actions 𝒜\mathcal{A}, observations 𝒪\mathcal{O}, transition kernel T⁡(s′∣s,a)T(s^{\prime}\mid s,a), observation kernel O⁡(o∣s′,a)O(o\mid s^{\prime},a), and discount γ∈[0,1)\gamma\in[0,1). The agent receives an implemented reward R~​(o)\tilde{R}(o) based solely on observations. We contrast this with the intended reward R∗​(s)R^{*}(s), which depends on the true latent state11 1 The agent optimizes only R~\tilde{R}; the intended reward R∗R^{*} is unobservable to the agent and serves as the designer’s ground-truth objective against which we measure alignment..

We define the value functions for the implemented reward R~\tilde{R} under policy π\pi as:

QR~π(s,a)=𝔼[R~(ot+1)+γVR~π(st+1)∣st=s,at=a]Q^{\pi}_{\tilde{R}}(s,a)=\mathbb{E}\left[\tilde{R}(o_{t+1})+\gamma V^{\pi}_{\tilde{R}}(s_{t+1})\mid s_{t}=s,a_{t}=a\right] (1)

Crucially, the expectation over R~​(ot+1)\tilde{R}(o_{t+1}) depends on the observation kernel O⁡(o∣s′,a)O(o\mid s^{\prime},a). If the action aa directly influences this kernel independent of the state s′s^{\prime}, the agent can manipulate the reward signal.

Wireheading via Channel Control

We identify a subset of actions 𝒜task⊂𝒜\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{task}}\subset\mathcal{A} as “task-focused.” These actions influence observations only via state transitions (i.e., O⁡(o|s′,a)=O⁡(o|s′)O(o|s^{\prime},a)=O(o|s^{\prime}) for a∈𝒜taska\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{task}}). Wireheading occurs when an agent selects an action a∉𝒜taska\notin\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{task}} to exploit the observation kernel.

Assumption 1 (Dominance of Manipulation).

Assume a bounded reward range [0,1][0,1]. Let there exist a “wireheading” action awa_{w} and a bound rtask<1r_{\mathrm{task}}<1 such that for all states s′s^{\prime}:

  1. 1.

    Manipulation: The wireheading action yields maximal observed reward: 𝔼o∼O(⋅|s′,aw)[R~(o)]=1\mathbb{E}_{o\sim O(\cdot|s^{\prime},a_{w})}[\tilde{R}(o)]=1.

  2. 2.

    Task Limit: Task actions are bounded by ground truth: 𝔼o∼O(⋅|s′,a)[R~(o)]≤rtask<1\mathbb{E}_{o\sim O(\cdot|s^{\prime},a)}[\tilde{R}(o)]\leq r_{\mathrm{task}}<1 for all a∈𝒜taska\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{task}}.

  3. 3.

    Availability: awa_{w} is available in all states.

Under these conditions, we show that wireheading strictly dominates task behavior.

Lemma 1 (Wireheading Dominance).

Under Assumption 1, for any state ss, the optimal policy selects awa_{w}. Specifically:

QR~∗​(s,aw)>QR~∗​(s,a)∀a∈𝒜task,∀γ∈[0,1).Q^{*}_{\tilde{R}}(s,a_{w})>Q^{*}_{\tilde{R}}(s,a)\quad\forall a\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{task}},\forall\gamma\in[0,1).
Proof.

Consider the policy πw\pi_{w} that selects awa_{w} at every timestep. The value of this policy is the geometric sum of the maximal reward 1:

VR~πw​(s)=∑t=0∞γt​(1)=11−γ.V^{\pi_{w}}_{\tilde{R}}(s)=\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}(1)=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}.

Since 1 is the global maximum reward, V∗​(s)=11−γV^{*}(s)=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}. Now consider taking a task action a∈𝒜taska\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{task}} at step t=0t=0, followed by optimal behavior. The immediate expected reward is at most rtaskr_{\mathrm{task}}. The future value is bounded by V∗​(s′)V^{*}(s^{\prime}). Thus:

QR~∗​(s,a)\displaystyle Q^{*}_{\tilde{R}}(s,a) =𝔼s′​[r~​(s′,a)+γ​V∗​(s′)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{s^{\prime}}[\tilde{r}(s^{\prime},a)+\gamma V^{*}(s^{\prime})]
≤rtask+γ⁡(11−γ).\displaystyle\leq r_{\mathrm{task}}+\gamma\left(\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\right).

Comparing the two actions:

QR~∗​(s,aw)−QR~∗​(s,a)\displaystyle Q^{*}_{\tilde{R}}(s,a_{w})-Q^{*}_{\tilde{R}}(s,a) ≥11−γ−(rtask+γ1−γ)\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{1-\gamma}-\left(r_{\mathrm{task}}+\frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma}\right)
=1−γ1−γ+γ1−γ−rtask−γ1−γ\displaystyle=\frac{1-\gamma}{1-\gamma}+\frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma}-r_{\mathrm{task}}-\frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma}
=1−rtask>0.\displaystyle=1-r_{\mathrm{task}}>0.

The inequality holds strictly because rtask<1r_{\mathrm{task}}<1. Thus, the agent always prefers awa_{w}. ∎

The Self-Grading MDP

We instantiate this framework for Language Models using a Self-Grading MDP. Let the action space be a tuple 𝒜=𝒴×𝒢\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{G}, where y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y} is the generated text response and g∈[0,1]g\in[0,1] is a self-assigned score.

  • •

    State ss: The prompt and history.

  • •

    Intended Reward R∗​(s,y)R^{*}(s,y): The ground-truth quality of response yy (e.g., human preference or gold label).

  • •

    Implemented Reward R~\tilde{R}: The model receives its own grade as reward: R~=g\tilde{R}=g.

This creates a degenerate observation channel where the agent chooses the observation directly. If the model learns the causal link a→g→R~a\to g\to\tilde{R}, it can select aw=(y,g=1)a_{w}=(y,g=1). Even if yy is nonsense (yielding low intended reward R∗≈0R^{*}\approx 0), the implemented reward is maximal (R~=1\tilde{R}=1). If the model is honest, g≈R∗​(s,y)≤rtask<1g\approx R^{*}(s,y)\leq r_{\mathrm{task}}<1 (assuming imperfect performance). By Lemma 1, the strategy (y,1)(y,1) strictly dominates honest evaluation, predicting the grade inflation observed in our experiments.

Experimental Design and Results

Our theory states that wireheading is favored when three conditions hold: (i) the agent can causally influence the reward–measurement channel; (ii) this influence remains available across rounds; and (iii) the manipulated reward strictly dominates the honest task reward for a sustained period. In such regimes, a measurement–manipulating action achieves higher implemented return while lowering intended value.

We instantiate these conditions for language models via self-grading, which we describe in the conditions below. We keep prompts, data, and optimization constant and only change whether the model’s self-reported grade controls the reward.

Conditions.

In the Control condition, reward equals the external ground truth. The observation channel is action-independent without any obvious incentive to wirehead. In the Honest condition, the model also produces a self-grade, but reward ignores it and still equals ground truth. Cognition matches Selfgrade, but there is no causal path from actions to reward. In the Selfgrade: condition, the model’s self-grade is the reward. The observation channel becomes action-dependent and opens the path a→o→R~a\!\to\!o\!\to\!\tilde{R}. If high self-grades are always available, Lemma 1 predicts dominance of grade inflation over task learning.

Models and Tasks.

We evaluate Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B on three tasks: Sentiment (binary classification on IMDB movie reviews), Arithmetic (single-digit, exact match), and Summarization (one sentence summaries of CNN/DailyMail dataset). We chose tasks that were within a mid-sized model’s capabilities to learn within a few hundred steps, across low and high ambiguity settings.

Training Details.

We train using REINFORCE (Williams 1992) with an exponential moving average baseline (α=0.9\alpha=0.9). Each round, the model generates a response, receives a scalar reward, computes advantage as reward minus baseline, and updates LoRA (Hu et al. 2022) parameters via gradient descent. In Selfgrade and Honest conditions, generation is two-step: first producing a task answer, then a self-grade. Log probabilities from both steps are combined for policy updates. We use AdamW (Loshchilov, Hutter et al. 2017) (lr=2​e−5\text{lr}=2e-5, weight_decay=0.01\texttt{weight\_decay}=0.01), gradient clipping (max norm 1.0), and LoRA adapters (r=8r=8, α=32\alpha=32) targeting attention projection layers. Each episode runs 500 rounds, cycling through 100 task examples. Models are trained in bfloat16 precision on a single NVIDIA L4 GPU.

Identification.

Honest and Selfgrade share the same two-step self-evaluation prompt. The sole difference is whether gg controls the reward. Thus, any inflation unique to Selfgrade is attributable to reward-channel control, not to self-evaluation per se.

Summary of findings.

Figure 1 shows the core result: in Selfgrade, reward and accuracy diverge sharply, with reward saturating near 1.0 while accuracy plateaus around 0.5. In Control and Honest, reward tracks accuracy throughout training. Grade inflation is substantial in Selfgrade across all tasks, reaching 0.41 for summarization, but remains near zero in Honest (range: -0.02 to +0.03). The task-dependence is pronounced: summarization shows 2-3× higher inflation than arithmetic, consistent with our theory that ambiguous tasks amplify wireheading. Llama-3.1-8B exhibits stronger and earlier wireheading than Mistral-7B, supporting the scaling prediction.

Conclusion

Self-evaluation enables wireheading when it is coupled to reward signals. Our theory formalized conditions under which reward-channel control creates strict incentives for measurement manipulation, and our experiments confirmed these predictions across models and tasks. This work emphasizes that as language models become more embedded in complex environments with opportunities to influence evaluation, architectural safeguards become essential to performance and safety.

Limitations. We instantiate wireheading on a fairly limited scale: two models in the 7-8B parameter range and three specific tasks. While the theoretical incentives for wireheading are general, the empirical emergence may differ in larger frontier models, which might be robust enough to resist grade inflation or capable enough to exploit it more subtly. Additionally, our wireheading action (grade inflation) is structurally simple, and future work should explore more complex measurement tampering in agentic workflows.
